The chemical form of the accumulated metals in prey is an important factor in controlling the assimilation efficiency of dietary metal by a predator, with the assimilation of metals being highest when the metal is bound to metallothionein or other proteins, or to organelles.
the assimilation of dietary metals by the predator Palaemonetes was affected by both the origin of the accumulated metals in the prey and the sub- cellular compartmentalization of the prey metals.

the chemical form of accumulated metals in the prey, Nereis diversi- color, affects the assimilation of these metals by the predator, Palaemonetes varian, and this assimilation efficiency is related to the amount of metal in metal-rich granules and the amount of total protein and metallothionein in the prey.

the trophic availability of metals in prey to a predator.

the chemical forms in which accumulated metals are stored and the trophic availability of these metals to predators.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the chemical form of accumulated metal in prey is a significant factor controlling the bioavailability to the predator, but that the relationship between metal bioavailability and chemical form is complex and not easily predicted.
the chemical form of accumulated metal in the prey (in this case N. diversicolor) is important in controlling its bioavailability to a predator (P. varians).
the assimilation of trace metals by a predator from prey is a complex function of many factors, which are not fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the chemical form of accumulated metal in prey is not the sole determinant of assimilation efficiency, but that the relative importance of different forms of accumulated metal will vary between prey-predator combinations.

the bioavailability of a metal in the diet is a function of the chemical speciation of metal in the prey, which is determined by the route and rate of uptake of metal by the prey and the subsequent subcellular compartmenta- lization of the accumulated metal.
the chemical form of the accumulated trace metals within the prey (Nereis diversicolor) is important in controlling bioavailability to the predator (Palaemonetes vari- ans).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemical form of accumulated metal in prey (e.g. MRG) can have a strong influence on assimilation by predators.
the chemical form of accumulated metal in prey is an important determinant of trophic transfer.

trophically available metal is a complex concept, and the fractionation of metal into different subcellular compartments is not a simple predictor of the bioavailability of that metal to a predator, although it does provide useful information.
